    What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the manufacturer's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
    • Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the manufacturer.
    • In a recent development, nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the manufacturer's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

    Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the manufacturer. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

    In a recent development, nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

    "Although we expect the manufacturer to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate fresh multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider remarked in a note Thursday.

    The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

    Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

    On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

    Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

    It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

    Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

    CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

    It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, stated CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

    "We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he mentioned.

    "However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

    CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person.".

    "There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he noted in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us.".

    Industry observers note that bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

    The real issue is just how much money the manufacturer will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

    "Substantial companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies.".

    — CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.
    • The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow.
    • According to recent reports, inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.

    The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is eight basis points lower than yesterday and 33 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.).

    According to recent reports, inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates. But depending on how markets react, we could actually see lower mortgage rates. Keep reading after the charts for all the details.

    Below are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for perspective.

    P.S. Markets will be closed tomorrow for Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, and mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

    » Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders.

    Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to fresh inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

    Like I mentioned above, it's not totally obvious where mortgage rates will head next. Let's walk through the two scenarios.

    Industry observers note that here's why rates could go up: This morning, we got October's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, also known as PCE. It's the last measure of inflation to come out each month, but it's also the Federal Reserve's preferred metric, so PCE gets a lot of attention.

    According to recent reports, the stats came in mostly as predicted, though it's not like the predictions were good — inflation's been overly strong for a while. But the core year-over-year figure, which came in a tenth of a percent over predictions, could prove troublesome. Core PCE removes categories that can be extra volatile, so it's considered a measure that shows the underlying trend. In this case, the underlying trend is Not Good.

    It's already pretty much a lock that we'll see a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December meeting, because yes, raising the federal funds rate is the Fed's main tool for taming inflation. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but a rate-hiking cycle from the central bankers definitely keeps upward pressure on borrowing costs.

    It has been revealed that on the other hand, here's why that same inflation data could help rates go down: Over the past several days, we've watched the stock market go on a wild ride, with the Anthropic IPO and the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Yesterday, things weren't looking good for tech stocks, and these inflation numbers could make it even worse.

    According to recent reports, the amount that tech companies have borrowed to fund AI buildout is a significant concern for investors, since companies will have to cover those costs before investors see any profits. It's already a substantial task, and if everything costs more thanks to inflation, it's that much harder.

    Industry observers note that this AI-related anxiety is rough on the stock market, but it's been a boon for Treasury bonds. More demand for bonds pushes up bond prices, which brings down bond yields (basically, the return investors get on a bond). Mortgage rates for 30-year loans are generally benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, so here's why you care about all of this: Lower Treasury yields means lower mortgage rates, too. If investors keep stressing about inflation eating into tech profits, we could see mortgage rates continue to move lower.

    That was a lot of info on inflation, but inflation's not the only major metric influencing rates.

    Let's back up for a second. The Federal Reserve tries to keep the economy steady by focusing on two key goals, often referred to as the Fed's dual mandate. One side is price stability — keeping inflation reasonable. The other is maximum employment, meaning those who want to work are able to find jobs.

    According to recent reports, next week we'll shift our focus to the employment side of the Federal Reserve's mandate, because the first week of the month is always all about employment data. On Tuesday, Dec. 1, we'll kick things off with the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS). JOLTS can tip us off to trends in the labor market; stuff like whether folks are leaving jobs voluntarily or if companies have openings that are going unfilled.

    Recent findings suggest that on Wednesday, payroll firm ADP will release its monthly employment stats. ADP is looking at its own payroll data to get an idea of how the job market is growing or contracting. The numbers don't include the public sector, but ADP often provides a preview of how the jobs report will go.

    It has been revealed that the Employment Situation Summary, better known as the jobs report, drops on Friday. This is the big one, since it tells us the nation's unemployment rate. The jobs report's other major stat is, similar to ADP, how many jobs the economy added or lost in the previous month. Unlike ADP though, the jobs report is inclusive of everybody in the public and private sectors.

    Recent findings suggest that lately the labor market's been looking super healthy, which is great news for the economy but less positive for mortgage rates. When hiring's strong, the Fed can feel safer raising the federal funds rate (that's the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers adjust). Higher rates tend to discourage businesses from borrowing and expanding, so if the job market's on shaky footing, the central bankers are going to be cautious about raising the benchmark rate.

    What we're seeing now though, where inflation is clearly the problem and employment's just fine, is a recipe for higher rates. Again, the Fed doesn't control mortgage rates, but the central bank being in rate-hike mode puts upward pressure on mortgage rates.

    If we were to see employment falter in this latest round of numbers, it still probably wouldn't change the Fed's strategy. That would be one poor month for the labor market versus months upon months of inflation running rampant — so yeah, they'll keep an eye on jobs, but inflation's still the scourge.

    Our most likely source of lower mortgage rates in the short term is what I described above; investors who are leery of inflation and the promise of AI looking to the safe harbor of the bond market.

    » Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates.

    With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.55% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

    In a recent development, also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

    Recent findings suggest that if the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

    NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a newly introduced home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

    Tech Report: The Biggest Mistakes Investors Make During a Market Crash, and How to Avoid Them.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (849 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that when the stock market starts falling, investors face a difficult test.
    • It has been revealed that but market crashes also create opportunities.
    • Often, it comes down to three mistakes: trying to predict the bottom, selling because of fear, and buying cheap stocks without understanding why they are cheap.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Lawrence Nga – Nov 26, 2026 at 7:01AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Amazon ›.

    Sources indicate that when the stock market starts falling, investors face a difficult test. A 10% decline can rapidly become 20%. Headlines grow increasingly negative, and even experienced investors begin to question their decisions.

    It has been revealed that but market crashes also create opportunities. Some excellent businesses become available at prices investors could only dream of during a bull market. So why do many investors fail to take advantage?

    Often, it comes down to three mistakes: trying to predict the bottom, selling because of fear, and buying cheap stocks without understanding why they are cheap.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest mistakes investors make is waiting for the perfect moment to buy. They want the market to fall further before investing. Then, when prices decline again, they become convinced that an even bigger crash is coming.

    Eventually, the market recovers, and they miss the opportunity altogether.

    The problem is that nobody knows where the bottom is until it has already passed. Consider an investor who wants to buy shares in a company trading at $100. The stock falls to $80, but the investor waits for $60. It then rebounds to $95.

    The investor was right that the stock had become cheaper, but waiting for the perfect price meant missing the opportunity.

    Industry observers note that A better approach is to focus on valuation rather than market timing. Decide what a business is worth and identify the price at which it offers an attractive potential return. If the shares reach that level, consider buying a portion of your intended position. If the price falls further and the investment case remains intact, you can consider adding more.

    This approach, often called buying in stages, removes the pressure to get the timing exactly right.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Watching a portfolio lose value is uncomfortable. When a stock falls 30%, investors naturally wonder whether they should sell before things get worse. Unfortunately, fear can make a temporary decline feel like a permanent disaster.

    The important question is not how much the share price has fallen. It is whether the business has deteriorated.

    Industry observers note that imagine owning shares in Amazon (AMZN -3.12%). During a recession, consumers may spend less, businesses may become more cautious, and technology stocks may fall sharply. But before selling, examine what is happening inside the firm.

    It has been revealed that is AWS still attracting customers? Is Amazon maintaining its competitive position? Are consumers still buying things online? If the long-term investment case remains intact, a falling share price alone may not justify selling.

    Of course, this does not mean holding every stock through every downturn. Sometimes a falling share price reflects genuine problems: Customers are leaving, competitors are gaining ground, debt is becoming difficult to manage, or management has made poor decisions.

    So what to do? Whenever a stock you own falls sharply, revisit your original reasons for buying it. Compare the latest business performance with your expectations.

    If the investment thesis is broken, consider selling. If the business remains healthy and the valuation is more attractive, holding or adding may make sense.

    A market crash can make almost everything look like a bargain. But some stocks fall for good reasons.

    A manufacturer might trade at just 5 times earnings, while its competitors trade at 20 times. At first glance, it looks cheap. However, what if its sales are declining, its debt is rising, and customers are moving to competitors?

    The low valuation may be justified because the business is losing its ability to generate profits. This is known as a value trap: A stock looks inexpensive, but its underlying business continues to deteriorate.

    Before buying a beaten-down stock, investors should examine at least four things:.

    According to recent reports, in short, don't buy a stock just because it has fallen 50%. Understand why it fell, examine its financial health, and decide whether the problem is temporary or structural.

    Nobody knows exactly when the next market crash will happen, how far prices will fall, or when the recovery will begin. Trying to predict all three is an unnecessary burden.

    Instead, investors should focus on what they can control: understanding the businesses they own, knowing their value, and maintaining sufficient financial flexibility to capitalize on opportunities.

    A market crash can be frightening, but it does not have to be destructive. The biggest winners are not necessarily investors who buy at the absolute bottom. They are often those who avoid panic, recognize genuine bargains, and have the patience to let good businesses compound over time.

    In a recent development, you don’t need a crystal ball to hold your own — just honest perspective from investors. So we asked our analysts how they’d build a portfolio from scratch, what drives their investing, and when a stock gave them the ick. Bring their answers to the table.

    Industry observers note that this one’s for the relative who just opened a brokerage account. Here’s how three analysts would start from scratch.

    If I were starting from scratch as an investor now, I would build a three-stock portfolio that offers stability, diversification, and growth. Here’s what I would go for:.

    As one of the more value-oriented investors on the Hidden Gems team, I have quite a few stocks in my portfolio that could be considered to be excellent “beginner” stocks. But if I had to choose just three to start a portfolio with, they would likely be Berkshire Hathaway (BRKB +0.37%), Brookfield (BN +2.13%), and Realty Income (O +1.18%).

    In reverse order, I would choose Realty Income because it’s an excellent compounder with a 30-year track record of excellent total returns, and Brookfield because it’s a great combination of reliable fee-based income and investments in some of the most promising types of real assets. Finally, Berkshire is like a well-diversified portfolio all in one stock, and I’ve said many times that if I could only own a single publicly traded organization, it would be the one.

    Sources indicate that each quarter, the Stock Advisor team builds our list of Foundational stocks: 10 stocks that can form the basis of a well-diversified Foolish portfolio. That exercise is essentially the same as deciding what to buy when starting from scratch. It should be no surprise then, that my answer is obvious: Amazon (AMZN -3.12%) and Vertex Pharmaceuticals (VRTX +0.04%).

    It has been revealed that both of these businesses bring scale, leadership, and a credible path to decades-long success. They balance sector exposure and business-model risk while still putting capital toward companies with clear competitive advantages that are representative of some of the best the stock market has to offer. Two stocks do not a portfolio make, but I believe this is a strong starting point for many investors.

    According to recent reports, we asked our analysts what’s driving their investing this year. Their answers are worth borrowing as you blueprint for 2027.

    I will soon turn 54, and while I still feel like a kid, the fact is I’m not getting any younger. While I still love finding and investing in those great growth stories, I’m also slowly moving into more of a “protect your wealth” mindset.

    Retirement isn’t even a word in my lexicon today; I love what I do and where I get to do it and will keep on doing it as long as the Fool will have me. But last year I set out to really focus on dividend exposure in my portfolio and 2027 is going to be another year where that remains a top priority. Rest assured I’ll be checking in on our Dividend Investor service quite frequently.

    I recently read a book called Sport’s Perfect Storm: An Industry Now Totally Adrift, by Roger Mitchell.

    This line caught my attention: “In everything, the past is always prologue.”.

    Sources indicate that after several years dedicated almost exclusively to reading investment books, this year, I’ve concentrated my leisure reading primarily on business history, and simply history. Learning about the past will give me a better perspective when investing for the future. Plus, this newly introduced focus feels particularly timely given that this year marks the 250th anniversary of American independence.

    In a recent development, as the late Charlie Munger once said: “There is no better teacher than history in determining the future. There are answers worth billions of dollars in a $30 history book.

    It has been revealed that I want to think through and take bigger, bolder investment decisions that will play out decades from now. I want to find the compounding decade busters! By doing the research and building the conviction, you can build the investment positions.

    It has been revealed that however, then it takes discipline and patience to see those investments play out over the next few decades. It’s often so counterintuitive: you get super excited about something new (the dopamine hit) and then you have to wait … and wait … and wait (the sugar crash). Rome wasn’t built in a day, and neither was a truly Rule Breaking portfolio.

    In a recent development, I turned 57 this year, which puts me within a decade of retirement. I also know that many workers are forced to retire sooner than expected. So it’s probably time for me to start reducing my risk by beginning to build a bond tent that will get me through the “retirement danger zone”: a time when a bear market could delay my plans or force me to sell investments when they’re down.

    It has been revealed that however, like many Motley Fool members, I much prefer investing in stocks, and see investing in cash and bonds as the equivalent of being forced to eat broccoli because it’s good for me. (I don’t like broccoli.) So I will spend this year finding the balance between being prudent and pushing the envelope.

    In a recent development, someone will ask if you’ve ever gotten one wrong. Here, three analysts share the moment a stock gave them pause, and what they did next.

    In a recent development, alphabet (GOOG -2.02%) is one of my oldest, high-conviction portfolio positions. However, there was a period where I (along with many other investors) was concerned that its core search infrastructure might be unprepared for an AI universe disrupted by ChatGPT, despite it having invented much of the transformer architecture behind modern AI.

    Industry observers note that today, Alphabet is positioning Google Cloud as a primary growth engine, with an impressive backlog largely driven by enterprise AI adoption, it’s designing its own AI silicon through its custom TPUs, and is successfully integrating AI tools that keep owners within the Google ecosystem. While capex is substantial, it has the margins and cash position to maintain its trajectory without compromising a profitable growth story, and that’s a value proposition I continue to believe in.

    Sources indicate that I first researched Pinterest (PINS +6.54%) in 2019 and was instantly enamored with the potential. The user base was smaller than other platforms, yet growing fast. And it was undermonetized. I called it an “exponential growth opportunity” because it could stack user growth on top of monetization growth.

    My investment thesis for Pinterest appears broken, which is why I finally sold last year. Plenty of smart Fools think I’m wrong, and that may ultimately prove to be the case. But its most recent quarter showed only 17% growth in ad impressions and a 4% drop in pricing. In my view, the platform is getting oversaturated with ads, and many advertisers still aren’t willing to pay a premium price after all these years.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve long admired Oracle’s (ORCL -5.13%) specialized “RDMA” server technology that’s so well suited to handle AI workloads, and in the several quarters since I finally bought in, my shares have appreciated handsomely. It’s loaded with debt however, and I’ve looked to super extended debt maturities as a mitigating factor. However, a slate of 2025 and 2026 borrowings for data center build-outs bent my buy thesis — I felt the “ick” after some back-of-the-napkin math!

    My thesis didn’t break, due to explicit capital allocation and free cash flow assurances the tech giant shared at its 2026 Investor Day in late October. But I continue to train a critical eye on capital expenditures, free cash flow, and the balance sheet strength of the cloud-based tech titans I own.

    None of the analysts claim to know where the market is headed next — and that’s the point. They focus on businesses, not stocks, and make investment decisions accordingly.

    According to recent reports, you can bring that exact discipline and mindset to Thanksgiving. If someone asks what the market will do in 2027, it’s fine to skip the guesswork. Shift the question instead and ask, which businesses they’d want to own for the next decade, and why.

    Ready for ‘The Great Lock In’? Viral Money Trend Can Improve Focus

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some new money goals and make progress toward them.
    • That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.
    • Sources indicate that “You’re probably not doing too much,” says Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some new money goals and make progress toward them.

    That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.

    Sources indicate that “You’re probably not doing too much,” says Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan. “It gets dark early. So those can be great months to lock into saving and not spend in excess.”.

    One important component of the Great Lock In is developing new routines that will last well into 2027, states Jordan Mangaliman, founder and fiduciary wealth advisor at GoldLine Wealth Management in Fullerton, California.

    “We want a long-term habit versus a Band-Aid fix,” he states. “In today’s economy, money goes in and out so blindingly fast.”.

    Ready to join the movement? Here’s how to get started.

    Recent findings suggest that what’s your money moonshot? Maybe it’s paying off all your credit card debt or purchasing a home. Or spending less than you earn. Defining it is the first step toward achieving it.

    “Spend a lot of time identifying what that goal is,” Baird indicates. “Everyone’s in a different position, so comparing yourself to what you see online might not be applicable.”.

    Even while setting ambitious money goals, it’s worth grounding them in reality, Mangaliman indicates.

    If you want to save a larger portion of your income, he suggests trying the latest saving pattern for a couple of months to see how it feels rather than saying you’ll do it forever and then getting frustrated.

    “It’s a marathon, not a sprint,” Mangaliman adds.

    Once you’ve outlined those significant goals for your Great Lock In, create a budget to help you achieve them, Baird indicates.

    He suggests combing through your previous credit or debit card spending to see where your money is going. Then you can decide what you want to change or shift. Using a tool like the 50/30/20 budget calculator can also help. This approach allots 50% of take-home pay toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings and debt payments beyond the minimum.

    Recent findings suggest that baird suggests including saving as a line item in your budget so you don’t forget to do it. “Building that cost into your budget will put you in a better position later,” he says.

    Any Great Lock In should include growing your savings, because that makes achieving other goals easier, Baird says.

    Recent findings suggest that “Maybe there’s something you could cut in the short term to build up that savings,” he indicates. Good targets include subscription services, food delivery, entertainment and travel costs.

    Saving more is especially challenging in today’s environment, when everyday expenses like gas are higher than they were a year ago.

    Baird claims that makes winter a good time to try to reduce costs. There can be fewer temptations to go out and spend money when the days are shorter and the temperatures are colder.

    Recent findings suggest that mangaliman recommends setting aside three to six months’ worth of expenses, although even a smaller amount is helpful. “Ultimately it’s about what you can afford,” he notes. “It’s the foundation of your financial house.”.

    Along with building savings, paying down high-interest debt is another pillar of the Great Lock In.

    With credit card interest rates higher than they were a few years ago, carrying credit card debt has gotten more expensive. “I would consider applying some savings to paying down debt, especially right now when your debt is costing you more than you can earn in savings,” Baird says. (You still want to reserve an emergency fund to cover unexpected expenses.).

    “High-interest debt is one of the biggest thieves of wealth,” Mangaliman indicates. And one way to avoid turning to debt again in the future is to build up that emergency fund so it’s there for you if you need it.

    It has been revealed that even when you are committed to a Great Lock In, some hiccups along the way are inevitable. Success depends on continuing anyway.

    Sources indicate that “It’s like a diet,” Baird says. “Just because you ate ice cream on a Sunday doesn’t mean on Monday you can’t go right back to being disciplined again.”.

    “Be kind to yourself and do everything in moderation,” Mangaliman suggests. Just wanting to improve your finances is already a great first step, he says.

    Industry observers note that in fact, he embraces the Great Lock In mentality himself. “There’s an old saying: It’s not how you start, but how you finish,” he states. “And you want to finish the year on a strong note so you carry those habits into 2027 and beyond.”.

    Addas a preferred source on Google.

    • By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 26, 2026 at 7:34AM EST.
    • Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang's saga just took another unexpected turn.
    • It's no secret that Wall Street loves founder-led businesses, but why is that?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 26, 2026 at 7:34AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

    Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang's saga just took another unexpected turn. Nvidia's (NVDA -3.91%) board unanimously voted to reinstate him as CEO, less than a week after explicitly saying it wouldn't. The message the board is sending is clear. Despite Huang's extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and with one of his subordinates, he is extremely valuable to the company. Just how valuable? The market's reaction to Huang's reinstatement gives us a clue.

    Sources indicate that jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

    It's no secret that Wall Street loves founder-led businesses, but why is that? There are several reasons. Let's discuss two of them. First, founders, who often own a substantial portion of the company, have a strong incentive to maximize shareholder value. Hired CEOs do too, to some extent. That's why equity-based compensation exists.

    Industry observers note that however, founders tend to have more skin in the game. They wouldn't just lose their job if their corporation failed, unlike many hired CEOs. They would lose a substantial portion of their wealth. Second, founders often have a much deeper knowledge of the business they created, its characteristics, risks, competitive advantages, etc. That may give them an edge in leading the business to greater heights. According to some research, founder-led companies generally outperform broader equities.

    Sources indicate that so, Wall Street's faith isn't blind -- it is backed by data. That brings us back to Huang. He helped found Nvidia in 1993 and made it one of the most valuable companies in the world, and the corporation at the center of the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Huang is one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in corporate America. That counts for a lot.

    That's why the stock soared about 31%, gaining nearly $1 trillion in a single session, after it was announced that he was coming back. It was the largest single-day market-cap gain in history.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Sources indicate that huang's return reduces the uncertainty tied to Nvidia's CEO search. Before the announcement, the market didn't know whether it would take six weeks or six months, and it was hard to reliably assign probability estimates to each outcome. The market abhors uncertainty, so the news had a major calming effect for many investors. That doesn't mean that Nvidia is out of trouble.

    According to recent reports, the company still faces major investigations tied to Huang's scandals, and the man is scheduled to testify before Congress soon. Still, with Huang at the helm -- and even accounting for ongoing regulatory probes -- the stock looks attractive. The first sign of that is Nvidia's financial results. In the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended on Oct. 25, Nvidia crushed expectations.

    The tech giant's revenue soared 103% year over year to $115.8 billion, with data center revenue rising 110% compared to the year-ago period. Nvidia's non-GAAP gross margin remains exceptional for a company of this size at 74.9%, versus 73.5% in the year-ago period. Nvidia's non-GAAP earnings per share jumped 111% year over year to $2.68.

    Recent findings suggest that the company's AI tailwind is not slowing down much, if at all. It expects $130 billion in revenue for its fiscal year 2027 fourth quarter at the midpoint, representing a year-over-year increase of about 91%. Sure, that's a lower year-over-year revenue growth rate than in its recent third quarter, and so is Nvidia's 2028 fiscal year guidance of 75% year-over-year revenue growth.

    According to recent reports, but investors should remember two things. First, Nvidia tends to post stronger-than-expected results. It has done so more often than not for the better part of three years. So, a predicted 91% year-over-year growth rate may turn into something above 100% -- in fact, the company's Q3 2027 guidance implied its revenue would increase by about 89.5% compared to the year-ago period.

    In a recent development, further, a decelerating growth rate may indicate tougher year-over-year comparisons rather than slowing demand for the tech giant's products. Nvidia clearly still has a large market to tap into, and with Huang back at the helm, it is as well-positioned as ever to do so. And even after its 31% jump, the stock is down about 36% from the all-time high reached a little over a month ago. At current levels, Nvidia stock remains a buy.

    10 stocks we like better than Coca-Cola ›.

    Recent findings suggest that I consider myself adventurous, but I often prefer boring when it comes to the stocks I own. I have my fair share of growth stocks, for sure, but my staple "boring" stock is Coca-Cola (KO -0.03%).

    Industry observers note that although Coca-Cola is up over 40% this year (as of Nov. 24), its main appeal has long been its dividend. It has increased its annual dividend for 64 consecutive years, making it one of the market's premier Dividend Kings ( companies with at least 50 consecutive years of dividend hikes). Considering that and its sustained success, it's a stock I'll never sell.

    It has been revealed that you can count on one hand the number of brands more well-known globally than Coca-Cola. Its products (especially its namesake soda) are available in virtually every part of the world, and its asset-light business model enables it to operate efficiently.

    Industry observers note that usually, if a organization wants distribution somewhere, it needs plants, warehouses, and delivery fleets in that market. In Coca-Cola's case, it relies on bottling and distribution partners to do so. Instead of owning factories and delivery fleets around the world, Coca-Cola sells concentrates and syrups to its partners and lets them do the heavy lifting.

    Keeping its business asset-light lets Coca-Cola maintain high margins and an ultra-safe dividend. You don't get to 64 years of dividend increases without consistent, high-margin cash flows.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Not many companies fit the "recession-proof" narrative, but Coca-Cola is one of them. Even when the economy slows and money is tight, people still buy their favorite Coca-Cola brands. That's the beauty of its brand moat.

    And despite being the undisputed leader in its space, Coca-Cola hasn't gotten complacent with its drink portfolio. It constantly refines its lineup to adjust to changing consumer preferences. Just six years ago, it had over 400 brands in its portfolio. Today, it has around half of that.

    When you have an option for virtually every occasion, you keep customers in your ecosystem. It's how the company has sustained success for so long.

    In a recent development, coca-Cola is a premium business that's priced like one. At the time of this writing, it's trading at 28.9 times its earnings, which is higher than its average over the past few years and higher than the S&P 500's (^GSPC -0.25%)23.7 P/E ratio. The stock is still a buy, but after a 40% run-up this year, the upside may be more limited. Luckily, that doesn't affect its dividend.

    Sources indicate that coca-Cola is always a good long-term investment, but with bear-market fears lingering, a short-term silver lining is that the stock typically outperforms the market during sell-offs. Past results don't guarantee future performance, but Coca-Cola has strong momentum at a time when the tech sector is dragging down the broader market.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.).
    • Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in?
    • According to recent reports, first, let's remember how we got here.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.).

    Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

    According to recent reports, first, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout swiftly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

    The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

    Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three notable forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:.

    This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

    For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

    The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

    Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

    The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

    The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

    That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

    One key clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

    Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

    We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

    The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

    Recent findings suggest that from here, it's all about the follow through. We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) just completed the largest IPO in history, raising around $93.5 billion at $83 per share.
    • Recent findings suggest that given that it's now one of the largest publicly traded companies in the world, you might assume its addition to the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) is imminent.
    • According to recent reports, when Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.30%) debuted earlier this year, there was a lot of discussion around how the major indexes would handle it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By David Dierking – Nov 26, 2026 at 8:03AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›.

    Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) just completed the largest IPO in history, raising around $93.5 billion at $83 per share. The stock closed Nov. 20 at $88.91.

    Recent findings suggest that given that it's now one of the largest publicly traded companies in the world, you might assume its addition to the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) is imminent. It isn't, actually, and won't be for a while. But the stock will show up in several other major indexes within days.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    According to recent reports, when Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.30%) debuted earlier this year, there was a lot of discussion around how the major indexes would handle it. Typically, companies go public at much smaller market caps, not with market caps over $1 trillion. Index committees needed to decide whether to "fast track" these mega IPOs into the indexes sooner, given their outsize influence.

    Several providers made changes. But Standard & Poor's did not. It elected to keep the existing 12-month waiting period and generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) income requirements -- companies need to be profitable in the most recent quarter as well as the sum of the past four quarters in order to qualify.

    Anthropic, so far, falls far short on the GAAP income requirement, reporting a net loss of roughly $104 billion in the first nine months of this year.

    Given these requirements, the earliest we're likely to see Anthropic in the S&P 500 is late 2027.

    The S&P 500 will actually be the exception, not the rule, when it comes to adding Anthropic.

    Recent findings suggest that the Nasdaq-100 index updated its inclusion criteria as a result of the SpaceX IPO. Now, if a company's entire market capitalization ranks within the top 40 current constituents in the index, it can be added to the index after just 15 trading days. Since Anthropic is listed on the Nasdaq, it could show up in the Invesco QQQ ETF (QQQ -0.65%) before the end of the year.

    Industry observers note that the Morningstar indexes, which acquired the widely-used CRSP indexes, could add Anthropic after the close of the fifth trading day. The Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI -0.18%) would be one of the biggest funds impacted by this. FTSE Russell works on a similar timeline.

    Recent findings suggest that A lot of index funds will weight stocks according to the number of publicly available shares, not necessarily the total market cap. Since only about 5% of Anthropic's total market cap is now traded publicly, its starting weight will likely be small. Vanguard has projected only a 0.055% to 0.15% weighting for Anthropic in the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF.

    When and if additional shares become publicly available, the anticipated weighting of these stocks would likely grow along with it.

    If you really want to own Anthropic, you should probably just buy Anthropic.

    According to recent reports, the stock won't show up at all in the S&P 500 for the foreseeable future. For many of the major large-cap indexes and corresponding ETFs, the initial weight probably won't get much above 0.25%. The exception might be the Nasdaq-100, the Invesco QQQ ETF, and the Invesco Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQM -0.66%). They could see an allocation closer to 1% given the more concentrated nature of that index.

    It'll likely be a similar story to what we saw when SpaceX went public: a lot of hype but minimal impact to the ETF marketplace and your portfolio in general.

    Long-term investors almost certainly shouldn't be making significant asset allocation changes based on this. Even if you want to overweight tech based on a belief that Anthropic might spark the sector, your tech ETFs aren't going to meaningfully change in the future.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (754 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nerdwallet ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: 4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.
    • Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year?
    • It has been revealed that but what about your money?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

    Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

    It has been revealed that but what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

    In a recent development, dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he remarked in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”.

    Don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:.

    In a recent development, last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, says Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

    If systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, noted Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good plan, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?).

    “My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson mentioned. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”.

    Industry observers note that if your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

    Recent findings suggest that “This is the step I push hardest,” Judge states. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”.

    Recent findings suggest that if you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” states Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”.

    Recent findings suggest that make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

    Keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

    Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

    Take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

    Recent findings suggest that and set a reminder to enhancement your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the big concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he states. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

    It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

    “The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” remarked Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (870 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Is Micron Stock a Buy After HPE Stated Memory Will Stay Scarce Into 2028?

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE +1.57%) told investors on Nov.
    • "We expect supply of memory, NAND, and many other critical components to remain constrained to at least the second half of calendar 2028," CEO Antonio Neri said on the company's earnings call that evening.
    • Industry observers note that that seems like good news for Micron Technology (MU -4.53%), which makes DRAM (the memory computers use while they work) and NAND flash storage chips.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Daniel Sparks – Nov 26, 2026 at 8:17AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Micron Technology ›.

    Sources indicate that hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE +1.57%) told investors on Nov. 23 that it still can't get all the memory chips it wants. And it doesn't think that'll change soon.

    "We expect supply of memory, NAND, and many other critical components to remain constrained to at least the second half of calendar 2028," CEO Antonio Neri said on the company's earnings call that evening.

    Industry observers note that that seems like good news for Micron Technology (MU -4.53%), which makes DRAM (the memory computers use while they work) and NAND flash storage chips. But the memory maker's shares slid anyway. Micron closed at $707.70 on Nov. 23, just before the call. As of this writing on Nov. 25, the stock traded near $550, less than half the $1,213.56 it closed at on June 25, its record.

    Meanwhile, BNP Paribas downgraded the shares, saying memory supply might catch up to demand a year sooner than it had thought.

    In a recent development, the tech firm remarked in March that DRAM and NAND make up over half the cost of the parts in a traditional server. And its inventory more than doubled in fiscal 2026, from around $6.4 billion on Oct. 31, 2025, to $11.8 billion by July 31 and $14.1 billion by Oct. 31, 2026.

    Industry observers note that HPE's timeline seems to have stretched, too. In March, Neri mentioned he expected high DRAM and NAND prices to "persist well into 2027.".

    In a recent development, CFO Marie Myers said the $14.1 billion inventory reflected higher costs for commodity parts like memory, purchases for customer orders, and what she called "strategic buys." She added that HPE's commodity costs climbed by significant double-digit percentages in 2026, and she expects smaller increases ahead. But smaller increases are still increases, not the price drops a glut would cause.

    It has been revealed that BNP Paribas thinks one could. In a note reported on Nov. 24, it cut its rating on Micron to neutral from outperform. It now says DRAM and NAND supply and demand might approach balance starting in mid-2027 and drive average selling prices down. It flagged risks to major cloud companies' data center plans for 2028 and newly introduced factory capacity coming online.

    Micron's stock dropped 11% that day, and again on Nov. 25, when research firm TrendForce said NAND flash might move into oversupply in 2027. TrendForce still expects DRAM to stay tight through 2027, and DRAM made up about three-quarters of Micron's revenue in fiscal 2026.

    Part of the new factory capacity BNP mentioned is Micron's own. Its first new fab in Idaho should start making wafers in mid-2027, and a facility in Taiwan should begin meaningful shipments around then too. But Micron notes output at a new fab ramps up over a few quarters. And its other planned fabs, including a second one in Idaho and a new NAND factory in Singapore, aren't set to start output until the second half of 2028 or later.

    According to recent reports, "[W]e do not have line of sight to when supply and demand will return to balance," management wrote about DRAM in Micron's prepared remarks for its Sept. 30 earnings call.

    HPE's 2028 date matches Micron's building schedule. BNP's earlier date seems to rely more on demand weakening.

    Industry observers note that micron's fiscal 2028 ends on Aug. 31, 2028, so HPE's outlook covers nearly all of the year. If the outlook holds, Micron could spend most of fiscal 2028 selling into a market still short on chips. If BNP is right, prices could be dropping for most of it.

    The stock price looks closer to the second case.

    It has been revealed that at roughly $550, Micron trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of about 7.4 on its fiscal 2026 results. Based on the average analyst estimate for fiscal 2028, the price is below 3 times earnings.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Even BNP sees Micron's earnings per share bottoming at $86 in 2029, over the $74.33 per share Micron earned in fiscal 2026 under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). The stock looks cheap even on that bearish estimate.

    Industry observers note that one buyer's view could be wrong, of course. But I think HPE's outlook undercuts the glut worries, especially for DRAM, Micron's largest business. A buyer still stocking up at higher prices is tough to square with a stock priced for falling memory prices by mid-2027.

    I'd consider buying some Micron shares here, in a position small enough to ride out more days like Nov. 24. If HPE starts pulling that 2028 date forward, like BNP just did with its own, I'd rethink that.

    • By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 26, 2026 at 8:32AM EST.
    • Stock market volatility has ticked up dramatically in recent weeks, with the hottest stocks suddenly becoming some of the most volatile.
    • Sources indicate that there are good reasons for Wall Street to be downbeat about PepsiCo.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 26, 2026 at 8:32AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than PepsiCo ›.

    Stock market volatility has ticked up dramatically in recent weeks, with the hottest stocks suddenly becoming some of the most volatile. If you are a long-term investor with a dividend focus and $1,000 to invest, you're better off taking a look at deeply unloved PepsiCo (PEP +0.88%). That will get you about seven shares.

    Sources indicate that there are good reasons for Wall Street to be downbeat about PepsiCo. However, the manufacturer's long and successful history suggests that investors who think in decades, not days, will be well rewarded. Here's why you should buy it before the start of 2027.

    Sources indicate that to get the bad news out of the way right up front, PepsiCo's business isn't doing particularly well right now. It isn't falling apart, either, but inflation, increasingly budget-conscious consumers, and shifts in consumer buying habits have taken a toll. In the third quarter of 2026, organic revenue growth was 3.1%. Coca-Cola (KO -0.03%), the tech giant's primary competitor in the beverage space, saw organic sales rise more than twice as fast, at 7%, in the same quarter.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    According to recent reports, simply put, investors are focusing on the industry leader and taking a show-me attitude with PepsiCo. You can see that in their valuations. For example, PepsiCo's dividend yield is 4.2% compared to Coca-Cola's 2.2%. Looking at more traditional valuation metrics, PepsiCo's price-to-sales ratio is just under 2x compared to a five-year average of 2.5x. Its price-to-earnings ratio is nearly 18x versus a five-year average of 25x. Coca-Cola's P/S ratio is 8x compared to a five-year average of 6.4x, and its P/E ratio is 28x compared to a five-year average of 26x. PepsiCo is cheap compared to its own history and relative to Coca-Cola.

    That stated, there are many reasons to like PepsiCo beyond valuation. For starters, as noted above, it isn't performing as well as Coca-Cola, but the tech giant isn't doing poorly. It is probably best to view it as muddling through a difficult period. It has done that many times before over the last 54 years. If that seems oddly specific, it is. That's the number of years this Dividend King has increased its dividend. Sure, that's a decade less than Coca-Cola, but it is hard to complain about PepsiCo's streak.

    Recent findings suggest that moreover, PepsiCo can stand toe-to-toe with Coca-Cola as a business. They are both industry leaders in brand strength, marketing prowess, innovation capabilities, and distribution. You aren't exactly stepping down to own PepsiCo. Meanwhile, PepsiCo offers you diversification that Coca-Cola does not. Coca-Cola is a beverage giant, but PepsiCo is a beverage giant (Pepsi), a snacking giant (Frito-Lay), and operates a large, well-respected packaged food business (Quaker Oats). For investors who value diversification, that may actually give it a leg up on Coca-Cola.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Sources indicate that meanwhile, it isn't like PepsiCo is sitting still and hoping conditions improve. It is actively working to shift its business in line with changes in consumer preferences. For example, it has acquired on-trend brands (Siete and Poppi), and it has been bringing out updated versions of existing brands, with a focus on healthier fare and protein. These are exactly the types of things that you would expect the company to do, but such moves can take time to play out.

    Sources indicate that if you are looking to buy a stock and see it go up the next day, PepsiCo won't be a good option for you. The turnaround could take a year or more. However, you'll be collecting an attractive 4.2% dividend yield backed by a Dividend King with an industry-leading business while you wait. For patient dividend investors, this could be a very compelling long-term opportunity.

    Early in the second quarter Wednesday night in NBA Cup group play, LeBron James pulled up from Broad Street.

    In a recent development, he drilled a 35-foot 3-pointer amid a torrid stretch that saw him make a trio of triples and score 14 straight points for the 76ers on Thanksgiving Eve. Before that sequence, the Sixers were trailing the Miami Heat by three points at Philadelphia's Xfinity Mobile Arena. Afterward, they were up eight.

    Sources indicate that while becoming the oldest player in NBA history to notch a triple double — at 41 years and 330 days old — James continued his recent hot streak from beyond the arc, going 4 of 6 on 3-point attempts. Philadelphia shot 14 of 35 from long range en route to a 111-104 victory.

    The Heat (10-7) would have clinched East Group B had they come out on top, but Philadelphia (15-4) denied Miami an eighth consecutive win, despite losing Jaylen Brown to a hamstring injury late in the first half and Joel Embiid being sidelined by illness.

    Nick Nurse's squad is now 2-1 in NBA Cup competition; Erik Spoelstra's Heat dropped to that same mark.

    It has been revealed that james finished with a season-high 25 points and 12 assists, plus 10 rebounds, with maybe his most notable dime taking place early in the fourth quarter. The 22-time All-Star revealed his elite court vision, timing a halfcourt lob perfectly to connect with VJ Edgecombe for a layup. James later dialed up an alley-oop for forward Dominick Barlow to throw down.

    In a recent development, edgecombe was among the Sixers players stepping up in the absence of Brown and Embiid, as Philadelphia protected its nine-point halftime lead and kept Miami at arm's length over the final two quarters. He had 18 points, and Tyrese Maxey poured in 30.

    The Heat, who wound up trailing by 16 late in the final frame, were led by Giannis Antetokounmpo, who clocked out with 32 points, 14 rebounds and 4 assists.

    In a recent development, kevin Durant is now one of five NBA players to score 33,000 points. The 38-year-old Houston Rockets forward achieved that feat on Wednesday night in a 116-104 home victory against the Phoenix Suns. He joined James, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Karl Malone and Kobe Bryant.

    Durant did so while piling up 20 points for Houston (14-5), which, despite already being eliminated from NBA Cup knockout-round contention, kept pace in the upper echelon of the Western Conference standings.

    It has been revealed that the Rockets improved to 2-2 in Cup group play, while the Suns (9-8) slid to 1-2. They, too, have been eliminated from knockout-round contention in West Group A.

    Along the way, Houston center Alperen Şengün passed Hakeem Olajuwon for the second-most triple-doubles in franchise history. Şengün, only 24 years old, secured his 15th performance of that kind with 23 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists.

    Late in the game, Suns wing Dillon Brooks got into it with Durant and was ejected after receiving his second technical foul of the night.

    Although the Minnesota Timberwolves lost LaMelo Ball to an ankle injury Wednesday, they held on to defeat the Oklahoma City Thunder 113-106.

    According to recent reports, jaden McDaniels came through, major time, in the West Group B matchup. In fact, by game's end, he was the third player in Wolves history to log at least 30 points, 10 rebounds and 5 assists in consecutive games. That elite organization also includes Karl-Anthony Towns and Kevin Garnett.

    After going for 34 points, 10 rebounds and 6 assists on Monday in a win over the Brooklyn Nets, McDaniels put up 32 points, 10 rebounds and 5 assists this time out versus the Thunder (10-9), who are 2-7 in their last nine games and eliminated from Cup knockout-round contention.

    In a recent development, minnesota (14-5), on the other hand, is atop West Group B with a 3-0 record. McDaniels beat the third-quarter buzzer with a ridiculous off-balance shot. A late 3-pointer from Wolves guard Ayo Dosunmu helped seal the deal.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Sean Williams – Nov 26, 2026 at 9:06AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

    It's been a wild couple of weeks for Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%), its shareholders, and Wall Street as a whole, to put it mildly.

    Following the admission of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, as well as allegations of two extramarital affairs with employees, Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, spurring an elevator-down move in his manufacturer's stock the likes of which have never been witnessed. Over 45 calendar days (ending Nov. 20), Nvidia lost $2.75 trillion in market value.

    It has been revealed that jensen Huang and Nvidia's board still have a big problem on their hands. Image source: Official White House Photo by Joyce N. Boghosian.

    Then came the 180 on Monday, Nov. 23, with Nvidia's board reversing course and reinstating Huang as CEO after just 11 days. President Donald Trump congratulated the board on "what I consider to be an absolutely great decision," with a White House spokesperson claiming the president was involved in Huang's reinstatement as CEO.

    While Huang's return does resolve some near-term concerns for Nvidia, a critical problem remains that won't be easy to tackle.

    In a recent development, nvidia didn't add more than $900 billion in market cap on Monday by accident. Huang has become the face of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out, and his presence keeps Nvidia at the center of this multitrillion-dollar revolution.

    Industry observers note that “The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World!” - President DONALD J. TRUMP pic.twitter.com/bKAxuMr9aA.

    Jensen Huang leading the charge also means that Nvidia's aggressive innovation timeline stays on track. The manufacturer intends to bring an advanced AI chip to market annually, securing its top spot in graphics processing unit (GPU) compute capabilities.

    In a recent development, perhaps most importantly, questions about the numerous circular financing deals Huang orchestrated are likely to die down. Nvidia has pledged jaw-dropping amounts of capital to neoclouds, hyperscalers, and large language model developers who, in turn, will purchase GPUs from the company.

    Huang's return, coupled with Nvidia's eye-popping growth forecast, suggests its stock is a bargain -- but that's not the full story.

    It has been revealed that jensen Huang's biggest challenge awaits. Image source: Getty Images.

    Although Wall Street cheered this reinstatement, Nvidia committed the ultimate investing no-no: it broke investors' trust.

    Among billionaire Warren Buffett's laundry list of investing quotes, he once stated that "It takes 20 years to build a reputation and five minutes to ruin it." This month, we've had Nvidia's CEO and co-founder admit to an extramarital affair, have seen several probes kicked off by regulators into Nvidia's accounting and operating practices, and watched the manufacturer's board flip-flop on the company's longtime boss over a two-week stretch.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    What investor trust had been engendered has arguably been lost or damaged, and there's no quick fix for rebuilding it.

    Industry observers note that this intangible damage over the last couple of weeks may slow future circular financing deals, even with Jensen Huang back at the helm, and could further contract Nvidia's already historically low earnings multiple. Until Nvidia rebuilds trust with Wall Street and investors -- and there's no set timeline for this -- the upside for its stock and its dealmaking capacity may be capped.

    #132042. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (630 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (630 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct.
    • However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive.
    • It has been revealed that buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession initiative, makes it worse.

    However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a significant haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the organization's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

    It has been revealed that buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options. Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

    It has been revealed that this prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

    This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

    By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.
